content: 1. The timing of introducing complementary feeding has been linked to childhood and adolescent adiposity, as explored in a study conducted at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts. 2. A study in South Jakarta, Indonesia, found an association between early childhood caries and feeding patterns in children aged 3 to 5 years. 3. Research in Taiwan revealed that infant feeding practices are associated with physician-diagnosed atopic dermatitis, based on a prospective cohort study. 4. A cross-sectional study in the Gaza Strip compared the nutritional status of preschool-aged children with their nutritional history. 5. A study in healthy infants examined the relationship between folate and cobalamin levels and breastfeeding and weaning practices. 6. Feeding patterns during infancy were found to influence BMI trajectories in a multi-ethnic prospective birth cohort study. 7. A 1954 study investigated the effects of early and late introduction of solid foods into the infant diet. 8. Research in Pakistan highlighted the impact of the weaning period on the nutritional status of children. 9. The introduction of solid foods was studied in relation to asthma and eczema in children, with findings published in 2004. 10. A study in rural Nablus, Palestine, identified the prevalence and predictors of iron deficiency anemia among infants. 11. Early infant feeding practices were linked to weight gain in a study published in 1978. 12. A large Chinese cohort study examined the relationship between complementary feeding and childhood adiposity in preschool-aged children. 13. The introduction of complementary foods and its relationship to food allergies was explored in a 2013 study. 14. A seven-year follow-up study in Dundee, Scotland, investigated the relationship between infant diet and childhood health outcomes. 15. Milk feeding and dietary patterns were found to predict weight and fat gains during infancy in a 2008 study. 16. A retrospective analysis in Europe linked infant feeding patterns to taste preferences in children and adolescents. 17. Early growth patterns and infant feeding were shown to impact body composition at three years of age in a British study. 18. High ponderal index at birth, feeding practices, and BMI in infancy were studied in a European cohort. 19. Social class variations were found to influence predictors of rapid growth in infancy and obesity at age three in a 2014 study. 20. Associations between infant feeding and timing of linear growth and relative weight gain were explored in a study on childhood body composition. 21. Risk factors for obesity in preschool children in urban China were identified in a 2011 study. 22. Early infant feeding practices were linked to BMI trajectories in the first five years of life in a 2019 study. 23. A study in rural Senegal examined the age of complementary food introduction and its impact on physical growth from 2 to 9 months. 24. Pneumonia prevalence and risk factors were studied in children under five living in slums in Dibrugarh, India. 25. Persistent malnutrition and associated factors were identified among children under five in Limpopo Province, South Africa. 26. Stunting and anemia were studied in children aged 6–23 months in Southern Ethiopia. 27. Infant feeding practices were shown to influence weight gain from birth to three years in a UK-wide prospective study. 28. Iron deficiency screening in the first three years of life was analyzed in a retrospective case study spanning three decades. 29. Factors influencing malnutrition among young children in rural Sarawak, Malaysia, were explored in a 2014 study. 30. Undernutrition and associated factors were studied in children aged 24–36 months in slum areas of Bahir Dar, Ethiopia. 31. The frequency of added sugar, salt, and fat in infant foods up to 10 months was studied in the nationwide ELFE cohort in France. 32. Infant feeding patterns were found to influence growth in children in American Samoa in a 1985 study. 33. The initiation of food supplements and cessation of breastfeeding were identified as determinants of weanling shigellosis in a 1993 study. 34. Stunting and its determinants were studied in children aged 6–59 months in Northern Ethiopia. 35. An ecological systems approach was used to examine risk factors for early childhood overweight in the UK Millennium Cohort Study. 36. Infant childcare was associated with feeding practices and weight gain among US infants in a 2008 study. 37. Breastfeeding and complementary feeding were shown to influence growth until 36 months of age in the Euro-Growth Study. 38. Early diet and allergy risk were studied in the GINIplus and LISAplus birth cohort studies. 39. Regional analysis in India linked infant and young child feeding practices to diarrhea prevalence. 40. Length and weight of very low birth weight infants at two years of age were studied in relation to complementary food introduction. 41. Exclusive breastfeeding, complementary food, and nutritional status of premature infants were studied in Indonesia in 2018. 42. Infant feeding practices and weight gain in toddlers born very preterm were explored in a pilot study. 43. The influence of weaning on growth and health up to 18 months was studied in a 2004 publication. 44. Premature birth was identified as an independent risk factor for early adiposity rebound in a longitudinal analysis. 45. The age of initiation and type of complementary foods were associated with BMI and weight-for-length at 12 months in preterm infants. 46. Feeding, growth, and biochemical studies were conducted in very low birth weight infants in a 1985 study. 47. Breastfeeding and complementary foods were shown to influence growth until three years of age in the Euro-Growth Study. 48. Clinical practice guidelines for feeding behaviors and weight-for-age at 12 months were analyzed in a secondary study. 49. Infant feeding and obesity at 11 years were studied in a prospective birth cohort in Brazil. 50. Anemia and micronutrient deficiencies were studied in infants attending primary healthcare in Brazil.
